title: The Threat Actor Landscape
description: Not all attackers are the same. They differ by motivation, skill, resources, and the targets they choose. Understanding who is likely to target you — and why — is the first step in building proportionate defences.

nodes.label: Script Kiddie
nodes.detail: Motivation: curiosity, recognition, disruption. Skill: low — uses pre-built tools without deep understanding. Targets: anyone vulnerable, no discrimination. Risk: high volume, low sophistication. Don't underestimate them — they cause real damage with tools they didn't write and don't fully understand.

nodes.label: Hacktivist
nodes.detail: Motivation: political or ideological goals. Skill: variable — some are highly capable. Targets: specific organisations for symbolic impact (governments, corporations, media). Common attacks: website defacement, public data leaks, DDoS. Examples: Anonymous operations against government targets.

nodes.label: Cybercriminal
nodes.detail: Motivation: financial profit. Skill: variable to high — organised groups operate like businesses. Targets: anyone with money or valuable data — healthcare, finance, retail. Common attacks: ransomware, financial fraud, data theft for resale. Some groups have customer support and negotiation teams.

nodes.label: Insider Threat
nodes.detail: Motivation: financial gain, disgruntlement, coercion, espionage. Skill: varies — but they already have access and institutional knowledge. Targets: their own employer. Most dangerous because they bypass perimeter defences entirely. Often goes undetected for months.

nodes.label: Nation-State / APT
nodes.detail: Motivation: espionage, geopolitical advantage, economic advantage, infrastructure disruption. Skill: very high — government-funded, long-term operations. Targets: governments, critical infrastructure, defence, technology companies. Characteristics: zero-day exploits, custom malware, supply chain attacks, years-long presence. SolarWinds (SUNBURST) is a textbook APT operation.

caption: Click each threat actor type to understand their motivation, capability, and typical attack patterns. Note how some types overlap — a cybercriminal may be recruited by a nation-state; an insider threat may be financially motivated or coerced.
